qs.q: Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of hypercalcemia in a patient with known advanced lung cancer?

Overproduction of PTHrP by the tumor
Direct bone lysis by metastatic disease
Production of calcitriol by the tumor

o: Metastatic calcification secondary to chronic hyperphosphatemia (e.g., in CRF)

es.q: During an autopsy, examination of a patient's lungs reveals centriacinar emphysema predominantly affecting the upper lobes. Compare and contrast this type of emphysema with panacinar emphysema in terms of its typical association and location within the lung.
es.m: Centriacinar emphysema is typically associated with cigarette smoking and primarily affects the upper lobes. In contrast, panacinar emphysema is associated with α1-antitrypsin deficiency and primarily affects the lower lobes of the lungs.

es.q: A histological section from a patient's lung shows patchy fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity and honeycomb change. What specific histological pattern is required for the diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), and what is the typical prognosis for patients with this condition?
es.m: The specific histological pattern required for the diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP). The typical prognosis for patients with IPF is a mean survival of 3 years or less.

es.q: Describe the three main types of emphysema discussed in the article, detailing their characteristic anatomical distribution within the lung and their primary associated etiologies.
es.m: 1. **Centriacinar emphysema**: This type is primarily associated with cigarette smoking and predominantly affects the upper lobes of the lungs. 2. **Panacinar emphysema**: This variant is linked to α1-antitrypsin deficiency and characteristically affects the lower lobes of the lungs. 3. **Distal acinar emphysema**: This type is associated with spontaneous pneumothorax and the formation of bullae.

es.q: A patient develops acute respiratory distress following severe sepsis, and chest imaging shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Outline the clinical triad of Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and describe the hallmark microscopic finding of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) in its acute phase.
es.m: The clinical triad for Acute Lung Injury (ALI) – in the absence of primary left-sided heart failure – includes: 1. Acute onset of dyspnea. 2. Decreased arterial oxygen pressure (hypoxemia). 3. Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph. The hallmark microscopic finding in the acute phase of ARDS, which represents diffuse alveolar capillary and epithelial damage, is Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD), characterized by the presence of hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls.

ai.summary: The lungs are the essential organs of respiration situated within the thoracic cavity, separated by the mediastinum. The right lung is shorter and wider, consisting of three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) divided by horizontal and oblique fissures.

sections.p: The lungs are the essential organs of respiration situated within the thoracic cavity, separated by the mediastinum. The right lung is shorter and wider, consisting of three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) divided by horizontal and oblique fissures. The left lung is smaller, has two lobes (superior, inferior) divided by an oblique fissure, and features the cardiac notch and lingula.

b: Apex: Projects above the first rib into the root of the neck.
Base: Concave surface resting on the diaphragm.
Costal surface: Adjacent to the ribs and intercostal spaces.
Mediastinal surface: Contains the hilum, where the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and nerves enter or exit.

sections.p: These are the functional, surgically resectable units of the lung, each supplied by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus and a tertiary branch of the pulmonary artery. There are typically 10 segments in the right lung and 8–10 in the left.

b: Functional: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the heart; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood.
Nutritive: Bronchial arteries (branches of the thoracic aorta) supply the lung parenchyma.
Nerve supply: Derived from the pulmonary plexuses (sympathetic and parasympathetic/vagus nerve).
Aspiration: More common in the right lung due to the right main bronchus being wider, shorter, and more vertical.
Pleural Effusion: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity, often settling in the costodiaphragmatic recess.
Lingula vs Middle Lobe: The lingula is a structural homologue on the left lung, whereas the middle lobe is a distinct third lobe on the right.
Epaterial vs Hyparterial Bronchi: Eparterial bronchi pass above the pulmonary artery (right side only), while hyparterial bronchi pass below it.
Auscultation: Breath sounds from the right middle lobe are best heard anteriorly, while lower lobe sounds are best heard on the posterior chest wall.
Radiology: The minor fissure is only visible on a lateral X-ray in many patients, potentially masking fluid collections in the horizontal plane.

faq.q: What are the primary differences between the right and left lungs?
faq.a: The right lung has three lobes and two fissures, while the left lung has two lobes, one fissure, a cardiac notch, and a lingula.
It is a pyramid-shaped anatomical unit supplied by a tertiary bronchus and a segmental artery, functioning as an independent surgical unit.

faq.q: What is the nerve supply to the visceral and parietal pleura?
faq.a: Visceral pleura is supplied by autonomic nerves (insensitive to pain), whereas parietal pleura is supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (highly pain-sensitive).

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Physical examination of the chest involves inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation. Each step provides crucial information about the underlying lung pathology. Remember to compare findings bilaterally and systematically.
b: Dyspnoea: Onset, duration, severity (e.g., can you walk up a flight of stairs?), aggravating and relieving factors, associated symptoms like wheezing or orthopnoea.
Cough: Productive or dry, colour and consistency of sputum (e.g., rusty sputum in pneumococcal pneumonia), timing (e.g., nocturnal cough in asthma), associated pain.
Chest Pain: Location, character (e.g., sharp, pleuritic), radiation, relation to breathing or movement, severity, associated symptoms like fever or haemoptysis.
Haemoptysis: Amount, colour (streaky, frank blood), duration, associated symptoms, any recent trauma or foreign body aspiration.
Systemic Symptoms: Fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue – these can indicate infection, malignancy, or chronic disease.
Risk Factors: Smoking history (pack-years), occupational exposures (e.g., asbestos, silica), past medical history (e.g., TB, HIV, asthma, heart failure), family history of lung disease.
Travel History: Recent travel to areas endemic for certain infections (e.g., TB, fungal infections).
Medications and Allergies: Current medications, including traditional remedies, and any known drug allergies.

b: Pneumonia: Clinical diagnosis often based on fever, cough, dyspnoea, and focal chest signs, confirmed by CXR showing new infiltrate. Severity assessed by CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >30/min, Blood pressure <90/60 mmHg, Age >65 years) to guide inpatient vs. outpatient management.

Tuberculosis (TB): Presumptive diagnosis based on chronic cough (>2 weeks), fever, weight loss, night sweats, and CXR findings (e.g., apical infiltrates, cavitation). Confirmed by AFB smear or culture from sputum. HIV co-infection significantly alters presentation and progression.

Asthma: Diagnosis based on recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough, especially at night or early morning, with evidence of variable airflow obstruction (e.g., spirometry showing reversibility). Severity classified by symptom frequency and lung function (FEV1).

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): Diagnosis based on chronic cough, sputum production, and progressive dyspnoea in a smoker or individual with significant exposure to biomass fuel, confirmed by spirometry showing persistent airflow limitation (FEV1/FVC <0.7 post-bronchodilator). Severity staged by GOLD criteria (FEV1 % predicted, symptoms, exacerbation history).

Lung Cancer: Diagnosis suspected based on persistent cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, and CXR/CT findings of a mass or nodule. Confirmed by biopsy (histology). Staging (TNM classification: Tumour, Node, Metastasis) is crucial for prognosis and treatment planning, often requiring CT, PET-CT, and MRI.

sections.p: Initial management for acute lung conditions focuses on stabilization and addressing the underlying cause. For chronic conditions, management is often long-term and aims to control symptoms and prevent progression.
b: **Airway, Breathing, Circulation (ABC) Assessment:** Always the first step. Ensure a patent airway, assess respiratory effort and oxygen saturation. Provide supplemental oxygen if SpO2 is below 94% (or target 88-92% in COPD exacerbation).

**Pain Management (e.g., in trauma):** For chest trauma, adequate analgesia (e.g., paracetamol, NSAIDs, or opioids if severe) is crucial for effective breathing and preventing atelectasis. Avoid over-sedation which can depress respiratory drive.

**Fluid Resuscitation (e.g., in shock):** For conditions causing hypovolemic shock (e.g., massive hemothorax), intravenous crystalloids (e.g., normal saline or Ringer's lactate) are administered to restore circulating volume. Monitor for fluid overload, especially in patients with cardiac compromise.

**Antibiotic Therapy (e.g., for pneumonia):** Initiate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin, ceftriaxone, or azithromycin depending on local resistance patterns and severity) for suspected bacterial infections, then narrow spectrum once culture results are available. Avoid unnecessary antibiotic use to prevent resistance.

**Bronchodilators (e.g., for asthma/COPD exacerbation):** Short-acting beta-agonists (e.g., salbutamol) and anticholinergics (e.g., ipratropium bromide) are used to relieve bronchospasm. Administer via nebulizer or metered-dose inhaler with a spacer.

**Corticosteroids (e.g., for inflammatory conditions):** Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone) are used for acute exacerbations of asthma or COPD, or for interstitial lung diseases to reduce inflammation. Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone) are for long-term control of asthma and COPD.

**Chest Tube Insertion (e.g., for pneumothorax/hemothorax):** For significant pneumothorax or hemothorax, a chest drain is inserted to evacuate air or fluid and allow lung re-expansion. Monitor drainage volume and air leak.
**Referral:** Patients with complex lung conditions, suspected malignancy, or those failing initial management should be referred to a pulmonologist or thoracic surgeon for specialized care.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding the adverse effects and interactions of common respiratory medications is vital for patient safety and effective management.
b: **Salbutamol (Short-acting beta-agonist):** Common side effects include tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, and anxiety. These are usually dose-dependent. Advise patients to use the lowest effective dose and report persistent symptoms. Avoid in patients with uncontrolled arrhythmias if possible.

**Ipratropium Bromide (Short-acting anticholinergic):** Can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention, especially in elderly men with prostatic hypertrophy. Advise patients to rinse their mouth after use. Caution in patients with glaucoma.

**Prednisolone (Systemic Corticosteroid):** Short-term use can cause hyperglycemia, insomnia, mood changes, and increased appetite. Long-term use leads to osteoporosis, immunosuppression, hypertension, and Cushingoid features. Taper dose gradually to avoid adrenal insufficiency. Monitor blood glucose and blood pressure.

**Amoxicillin (Antibiotic):** Common side effects include rash, diarrhea, and nausea. Advise patients to complete the full course. Watch for severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) and discontinue immediately if suspected.

**Ceftriaxone (Antibiotic):** Can cause gastrointestinal upset, rash, and rarely, C. difficile infection. Avoid co-administration with calcium-containing IV solutions in neonates due to precipitation risk. Monitor liver and kidney function with prolonged use.

**Theophylline (Bronchodilator):** Has a narrow therapeutic index. Side effects include nausea, vomiting, headache, arrhythmias, and seizures. Monitor serum levels closely. Many drug interactions (e.g., ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, phenytoin) can alter its metabolism, requiring dose adjustment. Avoid in patients with active peptic ulcer disease.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications and timely escalation of care are critical in managing lung diseases to prevent irreversible damage or death.
b: **Acute Respiratory Failure:** Characterized by hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mmHg) with or without hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg). Signs include severe dyspnea, cyanosis, altered mental status, and accessory muscle use. Escalate immediately for ventilatory support (non-invasive or invasive).

**Pneumothorax (Tension):** A life-threatening emergency where air accumulates in the pleural space under positive pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum. Presents with sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds, and hypotension. Requires immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion.

**Pulmonary Embolism:** Sudden onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxemia, often with risk factors for thrombosis. Can lead to right heart failure and shock. Escalate for anticoagulation, thrombolysis, or embolectomy depending on severity.

**Sepsis/Septic Shock:** Lung infections (e.g., severe pneumonia) can lead to systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and sepsis. Look for fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Escalate for aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and vasopressors if shock persists.

**Cor Pulmonale:** Right ventricular hypertrophy and failure due to chronic lung disease and pulmonary hypertension. Presents with peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and hepatomegaly. Escalate for optimization of lung disease management and consideration of diuretics or oxygen therapy.

sections.p: Various patient-specific and environmental factors can significantly alter the presentation, diagnosis, and management of lung conditions, requiring tailored approaches.
b: **HIV/AIDS:** Immunosuppression increases susceptibility to opportunistic lung infections (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, TB, fungal infections) and atypical presentations. Diagnosis may be delayed due to non-specific symptoms. Treatment requires specific antimicrobial regimens and often prophylaxis.

**Tuberculosis (TB):** Endemic in East Africa. Can mimic other lung diseases. Co-infection with HIV is common and complicates management due to drug interactions and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Always consider TB in patients with chronic cough, weight loss, and fever in endemic areas. Diagnosis requires sputum microscopy (AFB), GeneXpert, or culture.

**Malnutrition:** Weakens respiratory muscles, impairs immune function, and reduces lung capacity, increasing susceptibility to infections and worsening outcomes in chronic lung diseases. Nutritional support is crucial for recovery.

**Pregnancy:** Physiological changes (e.g., increased oxygen demand, elevated diaphragm) can alter lung function and disease presentation. Diagnostic imaging (e.g., X-rays) should be minimized or shielded. Drug choices must consider fetal safety (e.g., avoid tetracyclines).

**Diabetes Mellitus:** Increases risk of infections (e.g., pneumonia, TB) and can worsen lung function. Poor glycemic control can impair immune response and wound healing. Careful monitoring of blood glucose is essential, especially with corticosteroid use.

**Drugs and Herbal Remedies:** Certain medications (e.g., amiodarone, methotrexate) can cause drug-induced lung injury. Herbal remedies may interact with prescribed medications or have direct pulmonary toxicity. Always inquire about all medications and supplements.

**Alcohol Abuse:** Increases risk of aspiration pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and TB. Impairs immune function and can lead to malnutrition. Liver damage from alcohol can affect drug metabolism.

**Kidney or Liver Failure:** Impairs drug metabolism and excretion, necessitating dose adjustments for many respiratory medications. Can also cause pulmonary edema (renal failure) or hepatopulmonary syndrome (liver failure).

**Age Extremes (Children and Elderly):** Children have smaller airways, making them more prone to obstruction and rapid respiratory decompensation. The elderly have decreased lung elasticity, weaker cough reflexes, and often multiple comorbidities, increasing infection risk and complicating treatment. Drug dosing requires careful adjustment.

sections.p: Tailoring management strategies for specific patient populations is essential due to their unique physiological, immunological, and socioeconomic considerations.
b: **Children:** Respiratory infections (e.g., bronchiolitis, pneumonia) are common. Airway size is smaller, leading to quicker obstruction. Dosing of medications is weight-based. Early recognition of respiratory distress is crucial, as decompensation can be rapid. Avoid aspirin due to Reye's syndrome risk.

**Pregnancy:** Prioritize maternal and fetal safety. Avoid teratogenic drugs. Chest X-rays should be shielded. Asthma management aims for good control to prevent fetal hypoxia. Pulmonary embolism risk is increased. Close monitoring of oxygenation is vital.

**The Elderly:** Have reduced lung capacity, weaker cough, and often multiple comorbidities (e.g., heart failure, renal impairment). Increased risk of aspiration, pneumonia, and drug side effects. Polypharmacy is common, increasing drug interaction risk. Functional status and social support are important considerations.

**People with HIV:** Highly susceptible to opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, TB, Kaposi's sarcoma). Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is crucial for immune reconstitution. Drug interactions between ART and TB medications are common and require careful management. Prophylaxis against opportunistic infections may be needed.

**Low-Resource Settings:** Limited access to diagnostics (e.g., CT scans, advanced microbiology) and specialized care. Reliance on clinical assessment and basic investigations (e.g., chest X-ray, sputum microscopy). Emphasis on cost-effective, readily available treatments. Community health workers play a vital role in education and early detection. Challenges include drug avail

Light criteria for exudate: Pleural/serum protein ratio > 0.5, pleural/serum LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH.
Chest tube insertion site: 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior/mid-axillary line, superior border of rib to avoid neurovascular bundle.
Horner syndrome triad from Pancoast tumor: unilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

mnemonics.t: Right Anterior, Left Superior: describes the anatomical relationship of the pulmonary artery to the main bronchus at each lung hilum.
Vein, Artery, Nerve: describes superior-to-inferior neurovascular bundle orientation under the costal groove of each rib; needles are placed above ribs to avoid them.

vivas.q: A 16-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. BP barely obtainable, lungs clear, heart sounds barely audible. Most useful treatment?
vivas.a: Perform emergent decompression via subxiphoid pericardiocentesis or immediate resuscitative thoracotomy. The clinical picture is cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart tones, distended neck veins with clear lung fields), not pneumothorax.

vivas.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer develops hyponatremia with concentrated urine. What is the ectopic hormone responsible?
vivas.a: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) secretion caused by ectopic production of arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH).

vivas.q: Which is the MOST likely cause of hypercalcemia in a patient with known advanced lung cancer?
vivas.a: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) secretion, most classically seen as a paraneoplastic syndrome in squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, or osteolytic bone metastases.

vivas.q: Calcification in the lungs, blood vessels, and periarticular soft tissues is a hallmark of what pathophysiological process?
vivas.a: Metastatic calcification, typically secondary to chronic hypercalcemia or severe hyperphosphatemia seen in end-stage renal disease (tertiary hyperparathyroidism).

vivas.q: A 69-year-old woman has weight loss, painless jaundice, a pancreatic head mass, and liver/lung nodules. What cardiac abnormality is she most likely to develop?
vivas.a: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (marantic endocarditis), characterized by sterile platelet and fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves due to advanced cancer hypercoagulability (Trousseau syndrome).

vivas.q: Sinus venosus ASD is specifically associated with anomalous drainage of pulmonary veins from which lung?
vivas.a: The right lung, typically involving anomalous drainage of the right superior pulmonary vein into the superior vena cava or right atrium.

vivas.q: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung tumour. Which population is most characteristically associated?
vivas.a: Non-smokers, women, and younger individuals, typically presenting peripherally in the lung parenchyma.

vivas.q: The overall 5-year survival for all stages of lung cancer combined is approximately what percentage?
vivas.a: Approximately 15% to 20% across all clinical stages combined globally.

vivas.q: Compare and contrast centriacinar emphysema with panacinar emphysema regarding typical associations and distribution.
vivas.a: Centriacinar affects the respiratory bronchioles predominantly in the upper lobes and is heavily associated with cigarette smoking; panacinar uniformly affects the entire acinus predominantly in the lower lobes and is caused by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

vivas.q: A histological section shows patchy fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity and honeycomb change. What histological pattern is required for IPF?
vivas.a: Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) pattern, characterized by alternating zones of normal lung, fibroblastic foci, collagen deposition, and subpleural honeycomb cystic remodelling.

vivas.q: Describe the three main types of emphysema, detailing anatomical distribution and primary etiologies.
vivas.a: Centriacinar (upper lobes, respiratory bronchioles, caused by smoking); Panacinar (lower lobes/bases, whole acinus, caused by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency); Paraseptal/distal acinar (subpleural/apical, distal duct/alveoli, associated with spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults).

vivas.q: Outline the clinical triad of Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and describe the hallmark microscopic lesion.
vivas.a: The triad is acute onset hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio <= 300), bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, and absence of left atrial hypertension (non-cardiogenic). The hallmark microscopic lesion is diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) with hyaline membranes.

vivas.q: How does the anatomical relation of structures at the hilum differ between the right and left lung?
vivas.a: Right hilum has the eparterial bronchus superior, pulmonary artery intermediate/anterior, and hyparterial bronchus inferior. Left hilum has the pulmonary artery most superior, main bronchus intermediate, and pulmonary veins most inferior and anterior.

vivas.q: Why must an intercostal drain always be inserted above the rib border?
vivas.a: The intercostal neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery, nerve) runs along the costal groove on the inferior margin of the superior rib; inserting above avoids catastrophic hemorrhage or nerve injury.

vivas.q: What is the anatomical basis of Pancoast syndrome?
vivas.a: Apical lung malignancy invading the inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (causing Horner syndrome), T1/C8 nerve roots of the brachial plexus (causing inner arm pain and intrinsic hand muscle wasting), and adjacent subclavian vessels.

vivas.q: Where does aspirated foreign material lodge in a supine versus erect patient?
vivas.a: In a supine patient, it enters the superior segment of the right lower lobe. In an erect patient, it passes into the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe due to gravity and bronchial geometry.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old is stabbed in the left parasternal 4th intercostal space. Pulse 130, BP 70/40, muffled heart sounds, jugular veins distended, lungs clear bilaterally. Which intervention is most immediately life-saving?
o: Tube thoracostomy in the left 5th intercostal space
mcqs.e: The presentation is cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad), requiring rapid pericardial decompression, not a chest tube.

mcqs.q: A 58-year-old heavy smoker presents with confusion, lethargy, serum sodium of 118 mmol/L, and high urine osmolality. What is the most likely underlying malignancy?
mcqs.e: Small cell lung carcinoma is notoriously associated with paraneoplastic SIADH producing severe euvolemic hyponatremia.

mcqs.q: Which histological subtype of lung cancer arises peripherally and is most prevalent in lifelong non-smokers?
mcqs.e: Adenocarcinoma is the most common primary lung cancer overall and the most characteristic type in women and non-smokers.

mcqs.q: Widespread metastatic calcification in lung parenchyma, gastric mucosa, and kidneys is typically associated with which laboratory finding?
o: Marked hypercalcemia with elevated calcium-phosphate product
mcqs.e: Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues when calcium and phosphate concentrations are abnormally elevated.

mcqs.q: A chest tube is indicated for an expanding right hemothorax. To avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle, the trocar should pass:
o: Immediately below the inferior margin of the upper rib
Directly through the middle of the intercostal space
Immediately above the superior border of the lower rib
Directly adjacent to the transverse processes posteriorly
mcqs.e: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve lie in the subcostal groove at the inferior margin of the rib; inserting above the lower rib avoids them.

mcqs.q: A sinus venosus atrial septal defect located near the superior vena cava orifice is classically associated with which anatomical variation?
o: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return from the right lung
Atresia of the left main pulmonary artery
mcqs.e: Sinus venosus ASDs frequently involve anomalous drainage of right-sided pulmonary veins into the SVC or right atrium.

cases.v: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and right shoulder pain for 3 months. Physical examination reveals right pupil miosis, partial ptosis of the right upper eyelid, absence of sweating on the right hemiface, and wasting of the small muscles of the right hand.

qs.q: What is the unifying clinical eponym and the primary anatomical site of the lesion?
qs.a: Pancoast syndrome (superior pulmonary sulcus tumor) involving the apex of the right lung.

qs.q: Which neural structures are directly compressed or invaded to produce these signs?
qs.a: The cervical sympathetic trunk/stellate ganglion (producing Horner syndrome) and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1 nerve roots, causing hand muscle atrophy and pain).

qs.q: What initial imaging investigation should be performed at a district hospital?
qs.a: Posteroanterior and apical lordotic chest radiography to evaluate for apical opacity and rib or vertebral destruction.

cases.v: A 34-year-old male with severe peritonitis following a perforated appendix develops sudden severe hypoxemia refractory to oxygen therapy 48 hours postoperatively. Chest radiograph demonstrates diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates without cardiomegaly. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is normal.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis based on this clinical triad?
qs.a: Acute Lung Injury / Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).

qs.q: What is the classic histological hallmark underlying this syndrome?
qs.a: Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) with alveolar capillary congestion, intra-alveolar edema, and dense hyaline membranes.

qs.q: What physiological mechanism explains the failure of standard supplemental oxygen to normalize PaO2 in this patient?
qs.a: Severe intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting caused by alveoli that are flooded or collapsed, remaining perfused but unventilated.

mistakes: Inserting a chest drain below the 5th intercostal space, risking direct laceration of the liver, spleen, or diaphragm.
Confusing the surface landmarks of the lung margins (Ribs 6, 8, 10) with the pleural reflections (Ribs 8, 10, 12).
Assuming all lung cancer hypercalcemia is due to bone metastases, missing ectopic PTHrP paraneoplasia.
Inserting an intercostal drain along the lower border of a rib, severing the intercostal neurovascular bundle.
Diagnosing tension pneumothorax instead of cardiac tamponade in left chest trauma, missing Beck's triad with clear lungs.
Misinterpreting apical infiltrates as solely tuberculosis in a smoker with wasting and ptosis, missing a Pancoast tumor.
exam: A 16-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. BP barely obtainable, lungs clear, heart sounds barely audible. Most useful treatment? — Perform emergent decompression via subxiphoid pericardiocentesis or immediate resuscitative thoracotomy. The clinical picture is cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart tones, distended neck veins with clear lung fields), not pneumothorax.

A patient with small cell lung cancer develops hyponatremia with concentrated urine. What is the ectopic hormone responsible? — Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) secretion caused by ectopic production of arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH).

Which is the MOST likely cause of hypercalcemia in a patient with known advanced lung cancer? — Parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) secretion, most classically seen as a paraneoplastic syndrome in squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, or osteolytic bone metastases.

Calcification in the lungs, blood vessels, and periarticular soft tissues is a hallmark of what pathophysiological process? — Metastatic calcification, typically secondary to chronic hypercalcemia or severe hyperphosphatemia seen in end-stage renal disease (tertiary hyperparathyroidism).

A 69-year-old woman has weight loss, painless jaundice, a pancreatic head mass, and liver/lung nodules. What cardiac abnormality is she most likely to develop? — Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (marantic endocarditis), characterized by sterile platelet and fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves due to advanced cancer hypercoagulability (Trousseau syndrome).

Sinus venosus ASD is specifically associated with anomalous drainage of pulmonary veins from which lung? — The right lung, typically involving anomalous drainage of the right superior pulmonary vein into the superior vena cava or right atrium.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung tumour. Which population is most characteristically associated? — Non-smokers, women, and younger individuals, typically presenting peripherally in the lung parenchyma.
The overall 5-year survival for all stages of lung cancer combined is approximately what percentage? — Approximately 15% to 20% across all clinical stages combined globally.

Compare and contrast centriacinar emphysema with panacinar emphysema regarding typical associations and distribution. — Centriacinar affects the respiratory bronchioles predominantly in the upper lobes and is heavily associated with cigarette smoking; panacinar uniformly affects the entire acinus predominantly in the lower lobes and is caused by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

A histological section shows patchy fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity and honeycomb change. What histological pattern is required for IPF? — Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) pattern, characterized by alternating zones of normal lung, fibroblastic foci, collagen deposition, and subpleural honeycomb cystic remodelling.

Describe the three main types of emphysema, detailing anatomical distribution and primary etiologies. — Centriacinar (upper lobes, respiratory bronchioles, caused by smoking); Panacinar (lower lobes/bases, whole acinus, caused by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency); Paraseptal/distal acinar (subpleural/apical, distal duct/alveoli, associated with spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults).

Outline the clinical triad of Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and describe the hallmark microscopic lesion. — The triad is acute onset hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio <= 300), bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, and absence of left atrial hypertension (non-cardiogenic). The hallmark microscopic lesion is diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) with hyaline membranes.

How does the anatomical relation of structures at the hilum differ between the right and left lung? — Right hilum has the eparterial bronchus superior, pulmonary artery intermediate/anterior, and hyparterial bronchus inferior. Left hilum has the pulmonary artery most superior, main bronchus intermediate, and pulmonary veins most inferior and anterior.

Why must an intercostal drain always be inserted above the rib border? — The intercostal neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery, nerve) runs along the costal groove on the inferior margin of the superior rib; inserting above avoids catastrophic hemorrhage or nerve injury.
